opening_note: October is San Diego's second summer. Some years the hottest week lands now, when the wind blows in from the desert. But the harvest has moved inland — new dates, new sweet potatoes, heavy pomegranates, the last sweet peppers — and as the water cools, the local rockfish comes in. Everything below comes from one store, and it all keeps you cooking through the week.

field_notes.name: A new date isn't dried fruit.
field_notes.body: Most dates sit in storage for months. This fall's are softer, glossier, and taste like caramel instead of candy — squeeze the container and they give. If they're firm, dry, or have sugar crystals on the skin, they're last year's. The fresh ones are worth looking for in the bin you already shop.

field_notes.name: October is when peppers go in jars.
field_notes.body: Across the Balkans, autumn is ajvar season: red peppers are at their cheapest, and families roast them by the crate and cook them down into a relish that lasts into winter. You don't need a crate. Four peppers make a jar. It's the same impulse behind everything in this basket — buy it while it's here, and make it keep.

field_notes.name: Let the oven cut the kabocha.
field_notes.body: A kabocha is dense enough to be dangerous with a knife. Put it whole in a 400°F oven for ten minutes, or the microwave for three, and the skin softens enough to cut through safely. Don't peel it. Roasted, the skin goes tender and you eat all of it.

field_notes.name: Dry fish, hot pan, hands off.
field_notes.body: Fish sticks when it's wet or when you move it too soon. Pat it dry, salt it, heat the pan until the oil shimmers, lay the fillet down away from you, and leave it alone for three minutes. When it's ready, it lets go of the pan on its own. That's also the first step of every braise — you'll use it on bone-in chicken thighs once the evenings cool.

weekend_meal.name: Seared rockfish, brown butter, and the October salad.
weekend_meal.intro: One meal should feel like the reason you went shopping. In October, it's a fish most people walk past, seared hard in a hot pan and finished in brown butter — the one cooking lesson this month is built around.
weekend_meal.card_line: Rockfish, roasted kabocha, brown butter, arugula, pomegranate, dates
ingredients: Half a kabocha squash, cut into wedges
weekend_meal.ingredient_note: Everything here is on the shopping list. A pound of fish is dinner tonight and lunch tomorrow. If the counter is out of rockfish, any firm white fillet works the same way.
weekend_meal.method: Heat the oven to 425°F. Toss the kabocha wedges with olive oil and salt and roast for 30 to 35 minutes, until the edges are dark and a knife slides through. Meanwhile, salt the fish and leave it on a plate for fifteen minutes, then pat it completely dry. Heat a heavy skillet over medium-high with a thin film of oil until it shimmers. Lay the fillets in, away from you, and don't touch them for three or four minutes, until the edges turn opaque and the fish releases from the pan on its own. Flip, add the butter, and tilt the pan, spooning the foaming butter over the fish for a minute or two until it smells nutty and turns golden brown. Squeeze in half the lemon. Put the arugula, pomegranate, dates, and feta in a bowl and dress it at the table with olive oil, the rest of the lemon, and salt. Serve the fish over the kabocha with the brown butter spooned on top, the salad beside it, and ajvar on the table.

drink.name: Barrio Logan Jamaica
drink.intro: One drink. It's still hot, and the pomegranates just came in.
drink.method: Put the tea bags in four cups of cold water and leave them in the fridge overnight — cold-steeped, hibiscus comes out bright rather than bitter. Take out the bags. Press the seeds from one pomegranate through a strainer and stir the juice in, with sugar to taste; start with a quarter cup and stop when it's tart-sweet, not sweet. Pour over ice with a squeeze of lime and a spoonful of whole seeds. The pitcher keeps four days.

try_another_way.context: So the last glass isn't watered down.
If you want it closer to tart.

one_thing_to_notice.headline: A fresh fillet is glossy.
one_thing_to_notice.body: At the fish counter, look before you ask. Fresh fish is glossy and slightly translucent, with no gaps opening between the layers of flesh. Dull, dry, or separating means it's been sitting. Ask to smell it; it should smell like the ocean and nothing else. It takes five seconds and tells you more than any label.

kabocha-squash.name: Kabocha squash
kabocha-squash.tile_uses: Sheet-pan dinner, the warm plate, the weekend
kabocha-squash.why_now: Kabocha is the squash that comes after the thin-skinned early ones — dense, dry, and sweeter than butternut. It's picked now and actually improves after a few weeks on the counter, which makes it the first thing in the year you can buy in October and cook in November.
how_to_choose: Dark green, dull rather than shiny — shine means it was picked early
Heavy enough to surprise you
A dry, corky stem
A pale orange patch on one side is fine; that's where it sat on the ground
No soft spots anywhere
kabocha-squash.buy_this_much: 1 large, about 3 lbs. Half goes to the weekend, half to the week.
kabocha-squash.price_note: Sold by the pound. Usually the cheapest squash per serving in the store, because almost none of it is water.

kabocha-squash.weekend_use: Roasted in wedges, under the seared rockfish and brown butter.
kabocha-squash.storage: Whole, somewhere cool and dry for up to two months — it gets sweeter over the first few weeks. Once cut, wrap it and refrigerate; use within five days.
kabocha-squash.one_thing_to_learn: Kabocha is drier than other squash, which is why it roasts so well: there's less water to steam off before the sugars can brown. It's also why it can taste chalky if undercooked. Roast it until a knife slides in with no resistance at all, then give it five more minutes.
kabocha-squash.market_question: Do you have one that's been sitting a few weeks?

red-bell-peppers.name: Red bell peppers
red-bell-peppers.tile_uses: The ajvar, the sheet pan, raw with salt
red-bell-peppers.why_now: A red pepper is a green pepper left on the plant long enough to ripen, and by the end of the season that's most of what's left. Early fall is when California's red peppers are sweetest and often cheapest. By November they'll be shipped from farther away and priced like it.
how_to_choose: Glossy, firm, and heavy for their size
Deep, even red, with no green shoulders
Thick walls — press gently; they shouldn't flex
A green, fresh-looking stem
Blocky, four-lobed peppers char more evenly than twisted ones
red-bell-peppers.buy_this_much: 6. Four for the jar, two for the sheet pan.
red-bell-peppers.price_note: Loose peppers by the pound are almost always cheaper than the packaged bags.

red-bell-peppers.one_thing_to_learn: Green, yellow, and red bell peppers are mostly the same plant at different stages. Red ones have spent the longest ripening, which is why they're sweetest and cost more most of the year. The end of the season is when that extra time is cheap.

sweet-potatoes.name: Sweet potatoes
sweet-potatoes.tile_uses: Baked as dinner, the skillet hash, the sheet pan
sweet-potatoes.why_now: California's sweet potatoes are dug in September and October, most of them in the Central Valley around Merced, then stored through the winter. The new crop is on shelves now. It's the basket's filling one: a starch that keeps for weeks and makes a dinner on its own.
how_to_choose: Firm from end to end, with no soft or wet tips
Smooth skin, no sprouts or wrinkling
Medium and evenly shaped, so they cook at one speed
Orange-fleshed (garnet or jewel) for roasting
sweet-potatoes.buy_this_much: 4 medium. Two baked dinners for two, or one dinner and a sheet pan.
sweet-potatoes.price_note: Cheap now, and cheaper loose by the pound than in bags.

sweet-potatoes.storage: Somewhere cool and dark, not the fridge — cold makes the centers hard and off-tasting. They keep three weeks or more.
sweet-potatoes.one_thing_to_learn: A baked sweet potato is done well after it's merely soft. That's the starch turning to sugar, and it's the difference between a side and a meal.

arugula.name: Arugula
arugula.tile_uses: The warm plate, tacos, toast, the salad
arugula.why_now: Arugula is a cool-weather green. In summer heat it bolts and turns harsh; planted in September, it's ready in October with a gentler, peppery bite. It's the first green in months that tastes like it wanted to grow.
how_to_choose: Small leaves are milder than big, deeply lobed ones
Perky leaves with no yellowing
No wet or slimy leaves at the bottom of the bag or bunch
Bunches usually taste more of themselves than washed clamshells
arugula.buy_this_much: 2 bunches, or one big bag. It doesn't keep like the rest of the basket — use it first.
arugula.price_note: Bunches are often cheaper per ounce than clamshells.

arugula.one_thing_to_learn: Dress greens at the last possible moment. Salt pulls water out of leaves, and oil weighs them down, so a salad dressed ten minutes early is a wilted salad. Put everything in the bowl, carry it to the table, and toss it there.

fresh-dates.name: Medjool dates
fresh-dates.tile_uses: The warm plate, the salad, breakfast
fresh-dates.why_now: Nearly every Medjool in the country is grown in the desert two hours from here, in the Coachella and Bard valleys, and they're picked from late summer through October. The ones arriving now are this year's — soft, glossy, and much better than the ones that have been sitting since last fall.
how_to_choose: Plump and glossy, with skin that clings to the fruit
Soft enough to dent with a thumb
No crystallized sugar on the surface — that's age
If they're sold in a clear container, squeeze it; it should give
fresh-dates.buy_this_much: 1 lb. They last for months in the fridge, so this is more about having them than using them up.
fresh-dates.price_note: Bulk bins are usually cheaper than the boxed ones, and you can see what you're getting.

fresh-dates.storage: In the fridge in a closed container for up to six months, or the counter for a few weeks. Cold dates firm up; let them sit out before eating.
fresh-dates.one_thing_to_learn: A date is a fresh fruit that happens to dry well, not a dried fruit. Growers let them cure on the palm in the desert heat, which is why they're soft and sticky rather than leathery. Once you've eaten a new-crop Medjool, you'll notice the difference in the ones that aren't.

rockfish.name: Rockfish fillets
rockfish.tile_uses: The weekend meal, midweek fish tacos
rockfish.why_now: Rockfish is the local fish that gets more reliable as the water cools in fall: dozens of species, all mild and firm, and usually cheaper than salmon. It's sold at most fish counters in Southern California, sometimes as rock cod or Pacific snapper. This is the month to buy it instead of the usual.
how_to_choose: Glossy and slightly translucent, not dull or dry
No gaps opening between the layers of flesh
Firm enough to spring back when pressed
It should smell like the ocean, not like fish
Thicker fillets sear better than thin tail pieces
rockfish.buy_this_much: 1 lb at a time, twice a week: once for the weekend, once for midweek tacos. A pound is a big dinner and the next day's lunch. Fish is best within a day of buying.
rockfish.price_note: Usually well below salmon per pound. If the counter is out, any firm white fillet — cod, halibut — works in every meal here.

rockfish.storage: Cook it the day you buy it, or the next. Keep it in the coldest part of the fridge, on a plate, loosely covered.
rockfish.one_thing_to_learn: Rockfish cooks fast and forgives little, so it's the right fish to learn the sear on. It's done when the flesh turns opaque all the way through and flakes when you press it with a fork — usually three or four minutes on the first side and one or two on the second. When in doubt, take it off; it keeps cooking on the plate.
